title: Emergency Drugs in Pregnancy
sources: Critical Vector — Emergency Drugs in Pregnancy (10 scenarios; legacy FDA letters reproduced for cross-reference against Micromedex / Lexicomp / Briggs)
ACOG Committee Opinion 692 — acute-onset severe hypertension in pregnancy/postpartum
Enriquez AD et al. Arrhythmias during pregnancy (JACC-EP consensus tiers, 2021)
PROSPECT c-section analgesia (see the separate module); WHO PPH uterotonics + TXA; ASCIA anaphylaxis-in-pregnancy

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV Emergency Drugs in Pregnancy reference. Organized by what you're treating; the governing principle is that maternal stabilisation IS fetal stabilisation.

summary: Maternal haemodynamic stability is fetal stability — don't undertreat a genuine maternal emergency out of fetal-risk hesitancy. Every 'avoid' tier here still carries an 'unless life-threatening' escape clause. Position matters: manual left uterine displacement / left lateral tilt at ≥ 20 weeks during any resuscitation.

body.text: The FDA A/B/C/D/X letter system was retired in 2015 (replaced by the PLLR narrative summary) because clinicians read the letters as a linear safety grade they were never built to be — a 'C' can mean 'no data' just as easily as 'a worrying animal signal'. Legacy letters persist in Micromedex / Lexicomp / Briggs for older generic drugs and are noted below only for that cross-reference.

items: First-line is MAGNESIUM SULFATE, not a benzodiazepine — the one emergency scenario where the 'obvious' anticonvulsant is the wrong first move. Load 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min, then 1–2 g/hr infusion. Superior to phenytoin AND benzodiazepines for preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures.
Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output (loss of reflexes precedes respiratory depression). Antidote for Mg toxicity: calcium gluconate 1 g IV.
Second-line if Mg fails / contraindicated (e.g. myasthenia): lorazepam 4 mg IV or diazepam 5–10 mg IV. Then levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4,500 mg), then fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg for refractory.

body.text: Hypertensive emergency (SBP ≥ 160 or DBP ≥ 110 — treat within 30–60 min)

rows: 20 mg → 40 mg at 10 min → 80 mg at 10 min (max single) → repeat to cumulative 300 mg
Avoid in asthma / heart failure / bradycardia. Neonatal bradycardia if near delivery.
Higher risk of maternal hypotension than labetalol/nifedipine — have fluids and fetal monitoring ready.
10 mg PO, then 20 mg at 20 min if still elevated
Preferred when no IV access. Extended-release is maintenance ONLY, never acute. The Mg + CCB neuromuscular-blockade concern was not borne out in large reviews — but monitor.

body.text: ACOG: any of the three first-line agents is appropriate — choose on access and comorbidity, not superiority. Don't over-lower BP — placental autoregulation in severe preeclampsia is not well established and a fast drop can cause fetal distress. Methyldopa is maintenance only (onset too slow for emergencies).

Management is essentially identical to the non-pregnant patient. Epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM (1:1000) mid-outer thigh, repeat q5–15 min — do NOT withhold or under-dose over uterine/placental vasoconstriction concern; untreated hypoxia and hypotension are a far greater fetal threat. The ONE pregnancy-specific move: manual left uterine displacement / full left lateral tilt at ≥ 20 weeks to relieve aortocaval compression. Antihistamines and steroids treat the tail, not the airway or BP.

items: First-line: oxytocin continuous IV infusion (half-life < 10 min — needs an infusion, not a single bolus; watch for hyponatraemia with high-dose prolonged infusions) + tranexamic acid 1 g IV when blood loss > 500 mL (vaginal) / > 1,000 mL (caesarean) and bleeding persists — reduces PPH mortality.

Second-line — ASK 'asthma or hypertension?' BEFORE reaching: methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM (contraindicated in hypertension / preeclampsia — hypertensive/stroke risk; avoid IV) OR carboprost (15-methyl PGF2α) 0.25 mg IM (contraindicated in asthma — bronchospasm).

Succinylcholine 1–1.5 mg/kg (still ~86–90% of obstetric RSI; decreased plasma cholinesterase in pregnancy can prolong it somewhat) OR rocuronium 0.6–1.2 mg/kg (favoured generally, sugammadex for rescue — though sugammadex pregnancy data is limited).
Propofol ~1–2 mg/kg standard induction. Fentanyl standard dose but opioid clearance rises 60–70% in pregnancy, so the effect may be shorter than expected.
Ketamine: can increase uterine tone at higher doses — reasonable when haemodynamically unstable (haemorrhage, sepsis); discuss timing with obstetrics if delivery isn't imminent.
Left uterine displacement during and after induction prevents the aortocaval hypotension that gets blamed on the drug.
Oral first-line: pyridoxine + doxylamine (useless once vomiting prevents absorption).

IV escalation: ondansetron 4–8 mg (large Danish registry — no increased major-defect / stillbirth / preterm risk; a small cleft-palate signal the authors attributed to chance — reasonable first IV agent with a shared-decision note), metoclopramide 10 mg (EMA 5-day limit — extrapyramidal risk), then promethazine / prochlorperazine (higher dystonia risk).
Give THIAMINE before/with dextrose-containing fluids in a malnourished hyperemesis patient (Wernicke prevention), plus fluid resuscitation.
LMWH — weight-based therapeutic dosing; does not cross the placenta — first-line for treatment and prophylaxis throughout pregnancy.
Unfractionated heparin — preferred when rapid reversibility matters (peripartum, planned delivery, urgent procedure); frequent aPTT monitoring.

Warfarin — AVOID for routine VTE/PE (embryopathy, esp. first trimester). Remains preferred for MECHANICAL HEART VALVES (lowest maternal valve-thrombosis risk) — often first-trimester LMWH then back to warfarin, individualised.
DOACs — NOT recommended (placental transfer, insufficient data). A patient on a DOAC who turns out to be pregnant is a bridge-to-LMWH conversation, not 'continue and monitor'.

body.text: Governing principle: treat the mother as you would any patient — maternal stabilisation is fetal stabilisation. Give without hesitation: naloxone (titrate to respiration; may precipitate maternal ± neonatal withdrawal, but untreated hypoxia is worse), N-acetylcysteine (protective for the fetus too — fetal hepatotoxicity mirrors maternal), activated charcoal, 100% O2 for CO. Fomepizole preferred over ethanol for toxic alcohols. Physostigmine / flumazenil — the usual (non-pregnancy) contraindications apply; pregnancy adds none. See the Antidotes & Reversal Agents module for full dosing.
Antibiotics — several flip category by trimester

rows: Ceftriaxone: caution at term (theoretical neonatal kernicterus from bilirubin displacement)
Safe 2nd/3rd trimester — AVOID 1st tri (cleft-lip signal) and at term (neonatal haemolysis)
Check gestational age before reflex prescribing
Avoid unless no alternative for a serious infection

body.text: Safe: adenosine (6 mg → 12 mg, identical to non-pregnant; negligible fetal exposure), digoxin (levels run falsely high late in pregnancy — treat the rhythm), lidocaine, sotalol. Moderately safe: propranolol, metoprolol, labetalol, verapamil, procainamide, flecainide. AVOID (unless maternal life-threatening and refractory to everything else): amiodarone (fetal hypothyroidism, growth restriction, prematurity), dronedarone, dofetilide. Don't undertreat a genuine maternal arrhythmia — every 'avoid' still has the life-threatening escape clause.
